content.stem: A girl whose eyes are 1.5 m above the ground stands on level ground, 30 m away from the foot of a vertical building AB. From her eyes, the angle of elevation of the top A of the building is \(60^\circ\). Find the height of the building, correct to the nearest metre. (Take \(\sqrt{3} = 1.732\).)

diagrams.alt: A vertical building AB stands on level ground, with A at the top and B at the foot; its height is marked h. A girl PE stands on the ground to the right of the building, with her foot at P and her eyes at E; PE is labelled 1.5 m. The distance along the ground between the building and the girl is labelled 30 m. A dashed horizontal line from E meets the building at C, with a right angle at C. The line of sight EA rises from E to the top of the building, and the angle AEC between the horizontal and the line of sight is marked 60 degrees.
diagrams.solutionAlt: In step 2 the part AC of the building above eye level is highlighted; it is found to be 51.96 m, and adding CB = 1.5 m gives the height AB of about 53 m.

hints: The angle of 60° is measured at the girl's eye level, not at ground level. Which right-angled triangle has this angle?
Don't forget the part of the building below her eye level.

solution.modelAnswer: In right \(\triangle ACE\), \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{AC}{CE}\), so \(AC = 30\sqrt{3} = 30 \times 1.732 = 51.96\) m. \(AB = AC + CB = 51.96 + 1.5 = 53.46\) m \(\approx 53\) m.

steps.title: Choose the triangle
steps.explanation: The horizontal line of sight EC is 30 m long (equal to BP) and meets the building at C, 1.5 m above B. Triangle ACE is right-angled at C.

steps.title: Add the eye height
steps.explanation: CB equals the girl's eye height, 1.5 m. Round 53.46 m to the nearest metre.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to add the eye height 1.5 m, giving 52 m.
Using \(\tan 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) (confusing it with \(\tan 30^\circ\)), giving about 19 m.
Using sine or cosine instead of tangent when the adjacent side is known.

criteria.description: Forms the correct trigonometric ratio in the triangle at eye level
Adds the eye height and rounds correctly

questions.authorNotes: Exact height \(1.5 + 30\sqrt{3} \approx 53.46\) m. Tolerance 0.5 accepts 53 and the unrounded 53.46, but rejects 52 (eye height forgotten). The figure is drawn to scale (1 unit = 1 m), so the 1.5 m eye height appears small.

content.stem: T is the top of a lighthouse TF which is 90 m high above sea level, F being its foot. A ship sails directly away from the lighthouse. When the ship is at P, the angle of depression of the ship from T is \(60^\circ\); a little later, when it is at Q, the angle of depression is \(30^\circ\). F, P and Q lie on the same horizontal line. Find the distance PQ travelled by the ship, correct to the nearest metre. (Take \(\sqrt{3} = 1.732\).)
content.instructions: In the figure the angles of depression are shown at the ship positions as the equal alternate angles TPF and TQF.

diagrams.alt: A vertical lighthouse TF, 90 m high, stands at the left with its top T and foot F at sea level. A dashed horizontal line runs from T to the right. Two ship positions P and Q lie on the sea-level line to the right of F, with P nearer the lighthouse and Q further away. Lines of sight TP and TQ are drawn. Angle TPF at P is marked 60 degrees and angle TQF at Q is marked 30 degrees, matching the given angles of depression from T. There is a right angle at F. An arrow below the sea line shows the ship moving from P to Q, and PQ is the distance to be found.
diagrams.solutionAlt: In step 2 the distance FP is highlighted (found to be 30√3 m), and in step 3 the distance FQ is highlighted (found to be 90√3 m); PQ is the difference FQ − FP.

hints: The angle of depression from T equals the angle of elevation of T from the ship (alternate angles).
Find FP and FQ separately from two right-angled triangles, then subtract.

solution.modelAnswer: \(\angle TPF = 60^\circ\), \(\angle TQF = 30^\circ\) (alternate angles). In \(\triangle TFP\): \(FP = \dfrac{90}{\tan 60^\circ} = \dfrac{90}{\sqrt{3}} = 30\sqrt{3}\) m. In \(\triangle TFQ\): \(FQ = \dfrac{90}{\tan 30^\circ} = 90\sqrt{3}\) m. \(PQ = FQ - FP = 60\sqrt{3} = 60 \times 1.732 = 103.92 \approx 104\) m.

steps.title: Angles in the triangles
steps.explanation: The horizontal through T is parallel to the sea line FQ, so each angle of depression equals the alternate angle at the ship.
steps.rule: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.

steps.title: Find FP
steps.explanation: Triangle TFP is right-angled at F. Rationalise the denominator.

steps.title: Find FQ
steps.explanation: Triangle TFQ is right-angled at F.

steps.title: Distance travelled
steps.explanation: The ship moves away from the lighthouse, so Q is beyond P and PQ = FQ − FP. Round to the nearest metre.

commonMistakes: Adding FP and FQ (as if the ship were on opposite sides of the lighthouse), giving about 208 m.
Putting the angle of depression at the foot F instead of at the ship, which makes the ratio upside down.
Rounding FP and FQ to whole metres before subtracting (52 and 156 give 104 here by luck, but this habit loses accuracy marks elsewhere).

alternativeMethods.title: Isosceles triangle
alternativeMethods.description: \(\angle PTQ = 60^\circ - 30^\circ = 30^\circ = \angle TQP\), so triangle TPQ is isosceles and \(PQ = TP\). In \(\triangle TFP\), \(TP = \dfrac{90}{\sin 60^\circ} = \dfrac{180}{\sqrt{3}} = 60\sqrt{3} \approx 103.92\) m.

criteria.description: Identifies the angles of the right triangles using alternate angles
criteria.expectedEvidence: ∠TPF = 60° and ∠TQF = 30°, or correct ratios set up in triangles TFP and TFQ
acceptedAlternatives: Uses the angles directly at T with the complementary angles (30° and 60° at T between TF and the lines of sight)

criteria.partialCreditRules: Follow-through: if FP or FQ is wrong but PQ = FQ − FP is correctly computed from them, award this mark.

questions.authorNotes: Exact answer \(60\sqrt{3} \approx 103.92\) m; with 1.732 it is exactly 103.92 m. Tolerance 0.5 accepts 104 and 103.92. The figure is drawn to scale (FP = 51.96, FQ = 155.88, TF = 90 units). Depression angles are marked at the ship positions (alternate angles) because the two arcs at T would overlap at this size; the instructions line says so. Reviewer may want the 'Isosceles triangle' alternative included in the rubric's acceptedAlternatives explicitly.
